The bar chart compares how much money citizens in France and the UK spent on five different consumer products (cars, computers, books, perfume and cameras) in the year 2010.

Overall, it is clear that the UK significantly out spent France on most of the given categories, except for computers and perfume. Additionally, cars received the highest amount of expenditure in both countries, whereas perfume was the least consumed item overall.
The British spent the most money on cars, at over 450.000 pounds sterling, compared to around 400.000 pounds sterling in France.

There was also a big difference in camera spending, where British people spent nearly 350.000 pounds sterling, while France spent only about half of this figure.

The bar chart illustrates the proportion of households (which owned/ owning) cars in a European nation from 1971 to 2001.
The bar chart compares the proportion of households with no car, one car, or more than two cars in a European nation from 1971 to 2001.

Overall, it is clear that the percentage of households without a car experienced a significant decrease over the period shown. In contrast, the opposite trend was true for families owning either one car or multiple vehicles, with the figure for one-car households emerging as the highest by 2001.
In 1971, just under 43 percent of families did not have cars, which was the highest percentage among the three groups.
However, this figure decreased continuously in the following years, and by 2001, only 28 percent of families still did not own a car.
In contrast, the proportion of households with 1 car increased over the 30-year period, reaching the highest point at 46 percent in 1991, before dropping to 43 percent in 2001.
However, by 2001, this was the most common group in the country.
Meanwhile, the share of families with 2 or more cars did not follow a single trend. but changed over time.
It increased in the 1970s, and 1990s, but dropped between 1981 and 1991.
The bar chart shows the volume of carbon emissions generated by three types of fossil fuels — gas, oil, and coal — in the United Kingdom from 1990 to 2010.

Overall, it is clear that carbon emissions from all three fossil fuels were relatively stable over the 20-year period, except for some changes in 1995. Furthermore, coal consistently produced the highest level of emissions, followed by oil, while gas was the lowest contributor.
In 1990, coal was the main polluter, emitting approximately 315 million tons of carbon.
Oil came second with roughly 270 million tons, while gas was the least polluting fuel, with a lower figure of around 220 million tons.
Looking at the rest of the period, 1995 saw the only main change in the pattern.
Gas emissions went up to approximately 320 million tons before dropping back to around 220 million tons in 2000 and staying at this level until 2010.
In contrast, coal emissions decreased sharply to about 190 million tons in 1995, after which they recovered to roughly 315 million tons in the remaining years.
Meanwhile, oil emissions decreased slightly to around 240 million tons in 1995 and then returned to approximately 270 million tons from 2000 onwards.
The bar chart shows how much money was spent daily on three categories—food, entertainment, and transport—in three different areas (A, B, and C) in 2017.

Overall, it is clear that Area B spent the most money on all three categories, which was higher than the figures for Areas C and A. In addition, food was the largest expense in Areas A and B, while entertainment was the most popular spending category in Area C.
Looking at Area B, it was the biggest spender overall, with spending on food reaching $37 million.
Expenditure on entertainment and transport was slightly lower, at $36 million and $34 million respectively.
In Area C, entertainment was the highest at $35 million, followed by transport ($33 million) and food ($32 million).
Interestingly, Areas B and C spent almost the same amount of money on entertainment ($36 million compared to $35 million) and transport ($34 million and $33 million).
By contrast, Area A had the lowest spending in all three categories.
Food was still the main expense in this area, at $30 million, while figures for entertainment and transport were similar, at $28 million and $27 million in turn.
There was also a big difference in transport spending, where Area A spent $27 million, which was $7 million less than Area B.
The bar chart and pie chart give information about why US residents travelled and what travel problems they experienced in the year 2009.

It is clear that the principal reason why Americans travelled in 2009 was to commute to and from work. In the same year, the primary concern of Americans, with regard to trips they made, was the cost of travelling.
Looking more closely at the bar chart, we can see that 49% of the trips made by Americans in 2009 were for the purpose of commuting.
By contrast, only 6% of trips were visits to friends or relatives, and one in ten trips were for social or recreational reasons.
Shopping was cited as the reason for 16% of all travel, while unspecific ‘personal reasons’ accounted for the remaining 19%.
According to the pie chart, price was the key consideration for 36% of American travellers.
Almost one in five people cited safety as their foremost travel concern, while aggressive driving and highway congestion were the main issues for 17% and 14% of the travelling public.
Finally, a total of 14% of those surveyed thought that access to public transport of space for pedestrians were the most important travel issues.
The bar chart illustrates the reasons why US residents travelled, while the pie chart provides information about the main problems faced by them in 2009.
Overall, travelling to and from work is the primary reason for journeys, while the cost of travel is the biggest concern among the public.
In terms of reasons for travel, commuting to and from work accounts for the largest proportions, at 49%.
Personal reasons come in second place, with 19%.
Meanwhile, leisure and social trips represent smaller shares, with shopping at 16%, social or recreation activities at 10%, and  visiting friends or relatives making up only 6%.
Regarding the main issues for travelers, the price of travel is the most significant concern making up 36%.
Safety concerns rank second at 19%. Issues related to road conditions and transport include aggressive drivers at 17%, highway congestion at 14%, and access to public transport at 8%.
Finally, space for pedestrians is the least common problem, accounting for just 6%.
The bar chart illustrates the average electricity consumption per household in six countries while the pie chart shows the percentage of electricity generated from five different sources.

Overall, households in the USA consume the highest amount of electricity, whereas Indian households use the least. In terms of electricity generation, coal is the most common energy source, while hydropower provides the smallest proportion.
Regarding household electricity consumption, the USA ranks first, with an average of 12,000 kWh per household.
Germany and the UK follow in second and third place, with 8,000 kWh and 7,000 kWh per household respectively.
In contrast, the figures for China, Brazil, and India are much lower.
An average household consumes 5,000 kWh in China and 4,000 kWh in Brazil while India has the lowest figure, at only 3,000 kWh.
Turning to the sources of electricity generation, coal is the main source, accounting for 40% of the total.
Natural gas is the second largest contributor at 25%.
Nuclear power makes up 15% which is slightly higher than renewable energy at 10%.
Finally, hydropower produces the smallest share of electricity, at only 10%.

Finally, users aged 10 to 17 made up 14% and 15%, while the 65 and older group was only 8% on Facebook and 10% on YouTube.

The table illustrates the percentages of different types of households in a North American country in 1970 and 2003.

Overall, it is clear that family households accounted for a much higher percentage than non-family households in both years. In addition, married couples were the most common household type throughout the period, despite a significant decline.
In terms of family households, married couples made up the largest share, although the figure dropped sharply from 61% in 1970 to 41% in 2003.
n contrast, the other three categories in this group experienced slight increases of 1% each.
Specifically, households with a father and a child rose from 9% to 10%, while those with a mother and a child increased from 10% to 11%.
The proportion of other member sharing households also went up slightly from 13% to 14%.
Regarding non-family households, both categories grew significantly over the period.
Single-person households showed the largest increase, rising more than threefold from 4% in 1970 to 13% in 2003.

The bar chart compares how families in one country spent their weekly income across eight categories in 1968 and 2018.

Overall, food was the largest expense for families in 1968, but leisure became the highest spending category in 2018. In addition, spending on food, clothing, fuel, and personal goods decreased, while expenditure on housing, transport, and leisure increased.
In 1968, food had the highest proportion of weekly income, at 35%. However, this figure dropped significantly to about 17% in 2018.
In contrast, expenditure on leisure saw a big rise, increasing from around 9% in 1968 to roughly 22% in 2018, becoming the top spending category.
Similarly, spending on housing almost doubled, growing from about 10% to roughly 19%. Transport costs also grew, going up from 8% to 14%.
On the other hand, spending on clothing and footwear fell by half, from 10% in 1968 to 5% in 2018.
Expenditures on fuel and power, as well as personal goods, also saw small declines from around 7% and 8% to roughly 4% each.
Finally, the percentage of income spent on household goods stayed completely unchanged at about 8% in both years.
The bar chart illustrates the proportions of weekly income allocated to various household expenditures in a particular country in 1968 and 2018.

Overall, expenditure patterns shifted considerably over the 50-year period. While food dominated family budgets in 1968, leisure emerged as the largest spending priority by 2018. Furthermore, household goods was the only category whose share remained static throughout the period.
In 1968, food constituted by far the largest outlay, accounting for 35% of a typical household's weekly income.
However, this proportion experienced a substantial drop of more than half, falling to approximately 17% in 2018.
In contrast, recreational spending underwent the most pronounced increase, surging from around 9% to peak at roughly 22%.
Similarly, the proportion dedicated to housing virtually doubled from 10% to 19%, while the budget for transport rose steadily from 8% to 14%.
Regarding the remaining categories, expenditures on clothing and footwear halved from 10% in 1968 to 5% in 2018.
Marginal decreases were also witnessed in fuel and power, as well as personal goods, both descending from 7%–8% down to roughly 4%.
Lastly, the share of expenditure on household goods remained completely unchanged, holding constant at approximately 8% across both surveyed years.
The table illustrates the time men and women in the UK present on leisure activities each day in 2008, while the bar chart provides information about the time they spent doing household chores.

Overall, TV, video and radio took up the most free time for both men and women, while cooking and washing was the most time-consuming chore. In addition, men spent more time on leisure, whereas women spent more time on housework.
In terms of leisure activities, watching TV, video, or listening to the radio had the highest numbers, with 137 minutes per day for men and 118 minutes for women.
Reading was the second most common activity, taking 18 minutes for men and 19 minutes for women.
Finally, men spent 15 doing sport, while women spent slightly less time, at 11 minutes.
Regarding household chores, women spent much more time than men on most tasks.
Cooking and washing took the longest time, with about 76 minutes for women compared to only 31 minutes for men.
Women also spent more time shopping (about 36 minutes) and doing clothes washing and ironing (about 31 minutes), compared to around 26 minutes and 12 minutes for men respectively.
In contrast, repair was the only chore where men spent more time than women, at around 21 minutes compared to around 11 minutes.

In terms of leisure activities, TV, video, radio had the highest average minutes per day for both males and females, with 137 minutes per day and 118 minutes per day.
Reading made up the second share, 18 minutes per day for men and 19 for women.
The average number of minutes spent on sport activities in males were more than in females, with 15 minutes per day  for males compared to only 11 minutes per day for females.

Cooking and washing had the highest average minutes for males and females, accounting for 78 minutes per day with females and 30 minutes per day with males.
Shopping took 38 minutes per day for women and nearly 30 minutes per day for men.
The average number of minutes spent on clothes washing and ironing in females was twice as much as in males, with 30 minutes per day and 15 minutes per day respectively.
